title: Specification of Internet Transmission Control Program
summary: The first detailed specification of the Transmission Control Program, the ancestor of TCP, published in 1974. It describes a way to send reliable streams of data between hosts across interconnected networks. It is historic, and the later specification in RFC 793 replaced this line of work. It has also been formally marked historic by RFC 7805.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 675 describes an early Transmission Control Program for communication between processes on connected networks. It divides letters into packets and uses sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission, and flow control to deliver data in order; RFC 7805 later marked the memo Historic.

questions: what is the three way handshake
subtitle: A 1974 design for reliable communication between processes across connected networks.

tldr.problem: Processes on different packet-switching networks needed a way to exchange data despite loss, duplication, or out-of-order packet arrival.
tldr.mechanism: The Transmission Control Program uses sockets to identify endpoints, breaks letters into fragments, numbers packets, acknowledges data, retransmits unacknowledged packets, and regulates flow.
tldr.outcome: RFC 675 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 7805. It describes the December 1974 design, not a current transport specification.

sections.title: Letters, Fragments, and Connections
sections.content:
The document treats network communication as communication between processes. Each process can use ports, and a socket combines a network identifier, TCP identifier, and port name. A pair of sockets identifies a full-duplex connection.

Processes hand the TCP finite-length letters. The TCP breaks a letter into fragments when needed and places them in internetwork packets, which are carried in local packets through packet-switching networks. Gateways may reformat packets and may split a fragment for a network that requires smaller pieces.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs communicate through named endpoints called sockets. The TCP divides each letter into pieces when needed and sends those pieces across connected networks.

sections.title: Reliability and Flow Control
sections.content:
The Transmission Control Program is responsible for retransmitting unacknowledged packets, detecting duplicates, sequencing data, and regulating flow so a host is not overloaded. The RFC says these mechanisms keep letters on a connection in order.

The receiver advertises a window measured in octets. The sender does not transmit beyond the right edge of that window. At the receiving side, packets that arrive out of order are buffered until missing packets arrive so data can be delivered in sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver acknowledges data and tells the sender how much more it can accept. The sender retries unacknowledged packets, and the receiver puts out-of-order pieces back in sequence.

sections.title: The Internetwork Packet
sections.content:
The packet format includes an 8-bit information field, an 8-bit header-length field whose current value is 32 octets, a 16-bit text length, a 32-bit packet sequence number, a 32-bit acknowledgment number, a 16-bit window size, and 16 bits of control information. Control flags include SYN, ACK, FIN, DSN, EOS, EOL, and INT.

The acknowledgment number is the sequence number of the next octet expected. The window size is measured in octets. The packet also carries source and destination network, TCP, and port identifiers. A 16-bit checksum is present when the EOS bit is set.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet header identifies the connection, numbers the data, acknowledges what the receiver expects next, and advertises the receiving window. Control bits mark events such as starting or closing a connection.

sections.title: Opening and Closing a Connection
sections.content:
The two TCPs synchronize their initial sequence numbers using a three-way handshake. The RFC explains that a receiver cannot know from the first SYN alone whether it is an old delayed packet, so it replies with its own SYN and an acknowledgment that the sender verifies. The RFC's example then shows the sender acknowledging that reply and sending data.

The design also describes seven major connection states, including unsynchronized, SYN sent, SYN received, established, FIN wait, and FIN received. Either the local user or the remote TCP can begin closing with FIN. The RFC says details of resynchronizing a connection had not yet been specified.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends exchange and confirm sequence numbers before treating a connection as established. Either end can begin closing it, and the design keeps track of the connection's state during these steps.
